content:
On Thursday, alcohol distributor Southern Glazer’s announced that it reached a resolution with the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Alcohol and Tobacco Trade Bureau (TTB) in a longstanding investigation related to improper payments and bribery. In the deal, Southern agreed to pay $12.5 million. With this resolution the DOJ has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with the distributor, and the TTB agreed to take no further action regarding this case.

Last year, the U.S. government opened a federal investigation into the distributor regarding misconduct that occurred from 2016 to 2024. Former employees allegedly handed out cash payments, gift cards, luxury goods, golf trips, flights, and resort bookings for retailers in California for better shelf placement of Southern Glazer’s products and other benefits in return. The DOJ also says the company took out false invoices to conceal the payments.

“We are gratified to resolve the investigation in this fashion, and to be able to focus on earning the trust of our customers, supplier partners, and employees through ethical business practices, strong compliance oversight, and accountability at every level of the organization,” Southern Glazer’s president and chief executive officer Wayne Chaplin said in a statement released on Thursday evening.

In addition to the $12.5 million payment, Southern Glazer’s agreed to reinforce the company’s internal guardrails to prevent future misconduct. In the release, the company stated it had already made inroads to improve its TTB compliance after the federal investigation surfaced and prior to reaching the agreement. Southern Glazer’s claims it bolstered its staff and implemented proactive auditing, among other measures. The statement also suggests the non-prosecution agreement includes “other obligations over the next two years,” though the company did not disclose what those entail.

“This case serves as an important reminder that industry members are accountable not only for their own conduct, but also for the actions taken on their behalf by third party affiliates,” Anthony P. Gledhill, assistant administrator of field operations for the TTB said in a statement from the DOJ. “Third parties, likewise, are responsible for any illegal activities they carry out on behalf of an industry member.”

This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on harvest forecasts in France, Sapporo crossing the U.S.-Canada border, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • France braces for a record low harvest: After a growing season tempered by droughts and wildfires, producers in the country are expecting this year’s harvest to produce the lowest yields in 30 years. The French agriculture ministry forecasts a total of roughly 900 million gallons to be produced from this year’s harvest, a 6 percent dip year-over-year and a 17 percent drop from the average volume measured across 2021 to 2025.
  • Sapporo stokes the U.S.-Canada tariff fire: The Japanese brewer announced its plans to shift some of its brewing operations to the U.S. from Canada following the onset of a 50 percent tariff on Canadian beer. The move also comes after Trump issued a ban on Canadian alcohol imports, which is set to begin Sept. 29.
  • Dentist slashes world record Champagne sabrage: Swiss dentist Mirko Bozin broke the record for the number of Champagne bottles sabred in one minute. Bozin blew the tops off of 118 bottles in 60 seconds at a cutthroat tournament in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, breaking the previous record of 96 bottles that had been set just three months prior.
  • Kendall Jenner’s second bev-alc foray: The supermodel acquired a minority stake in U.K.-based functional beverage brand Trip.Trip launched in 2019 with cannabis-derived products but has since shifted its focus to other adaptogens, including non-psychedelic mushrooms.

Product releases to watch:

  • A new seat at the aperitivo table: The Campari Group, which dominates the Spritz sector with brands like Aperol under its wing, introduced a new aperitivo to the U.S.: Sarti. Though it was first founded in 1885, this marks its first appearance stateside, landing in markets nationwide. The blush-colored liquor blends blood orange, passion fruit, and mango flavors into a sweeter profile than the bitter qualities of Campari and Aperol.
  • Pappy to release 2026 Van Winkle Whiskey Collection: Crafted between the Old Rip Van Winkle Distillery and Buffalo Trace Distillery, this year’s lineup includes bourbons with age statements of 10, 12, 15, 20, and 23 years, along with a 13-year-old rye. Suggested retail prices range from $169.99 to $499.99. Bottles within the limited-edition collection will be available at select retailers and on-premise accounts nationwide.
  • Josh expands Reserve collection with Sauvignon Blanc: The California mega-producer added a Sauvignon Blanc from Sonoma County to its Reserve lineup. Josh Cellars Reserve Sonoma County Sauvignon Blanc is rolling out to retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $16.99.

content:
In 2026, it’s hard to think of a food that hasn’t been Dirty Martini-ified. The rise of the savory drinks trend over the past few years brought variations spiked with pickle brine, sungold tomatoes, and MSG, and flavors inspired by sour cream and onion chips, Greek salad, and brioche.

At Titán, the new bar and restaurant in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood, the tart, acidic flavors of escabeche are given the Martini treatment in the Dirty Root. But in making the drink, co-owner Ivy Mix and head bartender Sergio Sarmiento weren’t trying to follow the all-things food fad. Instead, they were looking to capture the signature briny flavors of a classic Dirty Martini while paying homage to the flavors of northern Mexico.

Titán is a collaboration between Mix and co-owner chef Alan Delgado. Both established themselves as masterminds of Brooklyn’s food and beverage scene in their own rights — Mix at bars like the beloved (and now-closed) Leyenda and Whoopsie Daisy and Delgado at Fort Greene’s Los Burritos Juárez, known for its hand-rolled flour tortillas and long lines.

Mix likes to think of a cocktail menu like a vinyl album: The whole should be better than the sum of its parts. Where the songs together to form a cohesive story in an old-school LP, the various drinks on a single cocktail menu should sing in harmony.

“When I make a menu, I have a spreadsheet of what kind of flavors we’re using, what kind of spirits we’re using, so I can see that I’m kind of covering the entire drink spectrum,” she says.

The Dirty Root was Titán’s answer to the Dirty Martini. While diners can order the classics, Mix likes to have her own versions of popular cocktails at the ready to point guests toward something new and unique.

“There are certain boxes that I want to check, so when people come in and ask for, for example, an Espresso Martini, we can say, ‘Do you want to try ours?’” she says. “The Dirty Root was the Dirty Martini box that we wanted to check.”

Though the Dirty Root resembles a Dirty Martini in its look and briny flavor, the ingredients are a far cry from the drink’s vodka-and-olive-brine roots. Bacanora — an agave-based liquor from northern Mexico’s Sonora region — and blanco tequila act as the base of the cocktail, with dry vermouth, carrot eau de vie, and carrot liqueur playing supporting roles. Rather than relying on the classic olives for the savory punch, Mix and Sarmiento looked to escabache, a piquant and spicy ensemble of pickled vegetables, usually including peppers, carrots, and onions, that’s a staple in many Mexican households.

“In pretty much all of the houses in Mexico, they have homemade chiles and vegetables in vinegar,” he says. “If you only have tortillas and beans, you can make tacos by adding the escabeche.”

Once the two brainstormed their vision for a Dirty Martini riff, Sarmiento began experimenting with making a carrot vinegar at home. While the root vegetables’ juice brings a burst of flavor on their own, Sarmiento needed to find a mixture that would complement the cocktail’s combination of liquors. After a series of trial-and-error, he landed on a blend of carrot juice, vinegar, sugar, and salt, with touches of turmeric and ginger.

“Then we put it all together, and you have this earthy, savory, northern Mexico-style Martini,” Mix says.

The striking drink presents in the glass with a bright orange hue and is served with a sidecar boasting a trio of garnishes: a lemon twist, a pickled carrot spear, and a cocktail onion. Mix shares that its appealing presentation spurs an onslaught of orders when it makes its way across the room, suggesting that it has somewhat of a “fajita effect” with customers.

“People definitely do that to this drink because the glass is sexy, it comes with a little sidecar, and the color is just really kind of light and beautiful,” she says.

The Dirty Root’s eye-catching appearance and complex flavor profile has propelled it to become one of Titán’s most popular orders. And consumers’ recent infatuation with Martinis — especially food-inspired ones — doesn’t hurt. But in conceptualizing the cocktail, Mix and Sarmiento never sought out to meet some kind of trend.

“There’s this fad going on right now, which is fine, where everything tastes like food,” Mix says. “Taking a food element was not the point. The inspiration for this drink is all of the flavors of the north of Mexico.”

content:
Is it possible that 2026 could eventually be looked back on as the make-or-break year for Scotch whisky?

In July, the U.S. finally lifted its 15 month tariff on Scotch, one that had contributed to a 15 percent decline in exports to this country, one of Scotland’s biggest international markets. Meanwhile, a new ​​U.K.–India free trade agreement introduced that same month could likewise prove transformational in opening up the world’s largest whisky market to more affordable Scotch.

And yet, many distilleries still remain on a sort of “pause” — Diageo and Brown-Forman operations of note — after the market became oversaturated post-pandemic, with a historic glut of liquid still building. Others, like Clynelish, have closed their visitors’ centers due to a lack of tourist interest.

On the positive, though, it seems that, thanks to a so-called “premiumization fatigue,” distilleries are focusing less on overpriced and ostentatious “clickbait” releases — your $200K Macallans for instance — and more on good, affordable, drinking Scotch. Indeed, this year’s tasting saw plenty of sub-$100, over-a-decade age-stated releases that snobs and newbs alike would be more than happy to have in their home bars.

From entry level offerings from the biggest names to more elevated releases from sleeper brands, exciting independent bottlings and a whole bunch of sherry bombs, here are VinePair’s 25 best Scotch whiskies for 2026.

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.
Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff samples thousands of bottles every year.

This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and — importantly — price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

For this Scotch roundup, all expressions were sampled in Glencairn glasses and allowed to rest for five minutes prior to tasting. We then evaluated the aromas, flavors, texture, and finish of each whisky. Unless there was something notably off or worrying about a whisky’s appearance — and on this occasion we encountered no such examples — we did not evaluate the products from a visual perspective.

How We Compiled This List

In order to provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Scotch whiskies to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

Not only would such an agreement contradict our editorial ethics and samples policy, it simply wouldn’t be possible to include everything we received. For this roundup, we tasted over 70 new submissions and also retasted more than a dozen bottles that were sent to VinePair throughout the course of the prior 12 months and that we were able to confirm are still available in retail channels.

During tasting, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based on the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria of 25 best Scotch whiskies to buy right now. It’s important to note that these are not just the highest-scoring bottles we tasted this year. Instead, this list showcases the best examples of Scotch across every price and for every scenario — because while price is completely objective, “affordability” is not.

The 25 Best Scotch Whiskies to Drink in 2026

The Best Scotch for Beginners

Glenmorangie Original 12

If “GlenMo” is no longer all that exciting to Scotch nerds, even they would have to agree there’s really nothing to dislike about this entry-level dram, especially at such a friendly price. It’s citrusy on the nose, with vanilla and sweet stone fruit on the palate, leading to a mildly spicy (cinnamon candy) finish. Despite the lower proof (40 percent ABV), there’s a creaminess of mouthfeel that makes this endlessly drinkable whether neat, on a cube, or even in cocktails. What can we say? This is just flawless single malt and a great place for a Scotch beginner to get started.

Rating: 91

The Best Blended Scotch

Compass Box Orchard House

Year after year, this category continues to be owned by Compass Box. (Quite frankly, we get very few blended Scotch submissions these days.) But despite the lack of competition, Orchard House shone brightly this year. This blend of single malt whiskies from Caol Ila, Clynelish, and several undisclosed distilleries was designed to be fruit forward as the name suggests and, indeed, it is apple-y on the palate, to the point of being almost brandy-like. A tad one-note, but never not delicate and delicious, this is a shining example of mastering a flavor profile through skillful blending.

Rating: 92

The Best Peated Scotch

Kilchoman Sanaig

One of the more slept-on distilleries on the island of Islay, Kilchoman quietly continues to put out some of the best releases in the region. Named after an inlet on the island, Sanaig is produced from a vatting of ex-bourbon and sherry casks, specifically Oloroso. The dried fruit/baking spice barrel notes meld beautifully with the smoke, making for a peated whiskey that is both accessible to newbies to the category, yet pleasing in complexity to longtime fans.

Average price: $76
Rating: 95

See Review

The Best Scotch to Seek Out and Splurge On

Bowmore 21-Year-Old Sherry Oak Cask

This new release to the U.S. market from the longtime Islay stalwart is aged in ex-bourbon and Oloroso sherry casks before being finished in first fill Pedro Ximénez (PX) sherry casks. Much milder in peated notes than its Islay brethren, the nose is floral and almost saison-like, though the palate is rich in toffee, maple syrup, and pipe tobacco. The finish offers almost rum ester-like pineapple/banana/tropical notes, before there is a lingering pink bubblegum sweetness. Sublime.

Average price: $450
Rating: 96

See Review

The Best of the Rest

The Best Scotch Whisky Under $50

Isle of Skye Rum Cask Finish

If the independent, family-owned Ian Macleod Distillers has the 2nd most expensive ($400!) whisky on this year’s list, they also have, by far, the most affordable, with this unfathomably price-undercutting 10-year age-stated marvel. The limited release blended Scotch is finished in Caribbean rum casks, though it’s hardly a “rum lover’s whiskey.” The tropical and spicy notes of the rum barrel meld well with the maltiness and slight peat of the Scotch for a balanced, flavorful pour. Enjoyable neat, it would soar in a highball with soda water or Coke.

Average price: $28
Rating: 90

See Review

The Best Scotch Whiskies Under $100

The Glengarry 12 Year

The leads are strong on this easy-drinker from the Loch Lomond Distillery. A palate of honey-dipped apple, a little cinnamon, and buttered biscuits make for an unfussy, everyday pour. There’s nothing to think too much about here — just enjoy your Scotch.

Average price: $52
Rating: 91

See Review

The Glenlivet 12 Year Old Provence Edition

If this household name is often overlooked by the experts, this new limited release is quite a bit more exciting. The classic Speyside single malt is finished in previously unused French sweet wine casks and Provence Cru Classé wine casks, creating an incredibly floral nose with a more fruity, juicy palate.

Average price: $55
Rating: 91

See Review

Jura 14 Year

Aged in American rye casks, this is one of the spicier single malts you’ll encounter. There are notes of red berries, vanilla, green pepper, and rock candy. Despite the minimal proof (40 percent ABV), it remains well-rounded with a rich mouthfeel.

Average price: $60
Rating: 92

See Review

Glenfiddich 14 Year Old

Yet another extremely accessible great-for-beginners Scotch that is, quite frankly, every bit as good as the brand’s higher price, higher age-stated offerings. Matured in ex-bourbon barrels, this is a no-frills expression of (perhaps) the Scotch world’s most famous single malt. Baked apple pie with caramel sauce and just enough oak to keep things balanced, this is easy-drinking and hard not to like.

Average price: $60
Rating: 90

See Review

Lagavulin 11 Year Old Sweet Peat Islay

The first permanent offering from the brand in nearly a decade, this 11 year old was mostly slept on by the press (including us!) upon its release earlier this year. But mea culpa, this is stellar. Aged entirely in first-fill bourbon barrels with a more mild peat content, it’s extremely fragrant on the nose, slightly smoky with some berry fruitiness; the palate is syrupy with strong notes of those strawberry hard candies from grandma’s house, leading into a delicious bubblegum sweetness on the finish that leaves you wanting more. Very approachable and enjoyable.

Average price: $70
Rating: 93

See Review

Benriach The Smoky Twelve

If Benriach is most known for its sherried single malts, this one is proof that the Speyside distillery can also play ball in the peat game. Built from a combination of peated and unpeated whisky aged in ex-bourbon barrels, sherry casks, and Marsala wine casks, the smoke mainly lingers in the background, balancing out all the fruity sweetness. Endlessly complex and surely a gamechanger for self-proclaimed “peat haters,” there are prominent notes of chocolate, orange marmalade, and barbecue potato chips.

Average price: $75
Rating: 92

See Review

Laphroaig 15-Year-Old

The first of two new(ish) 15-year-old Islays on our list, Laphroaig’s is actually a return to the brand’s core lineup after a decade-long absence. For about 25 extra bucks you get five more years of age compared to the flagship Laphroaig 10-Year-Old and those years are well worth it; the more aggressive peat notes are sanded down to something a little quieter and relaxed. There are maritime notes on the palate, a kiss of peaches ‘n’ cream, and a slightly sweet, oaky finish.

Average price: $89
Rating: 93

See Review

Ardbeg Trudernish 15 Years Old

If Laphroaig’s was a beloved return, down-the-block neighbor Ardbeg’s 15-year-old is the first of that age statement in their permanent lineup. Matured in ex-bourbon, new charred oak, and Oloroso sherry casks, it offers more of those classic nutty and dried fruit notes (think: figs, raisins, apricots). But it’s also earthy and smoky as expected, though always in balance. At this price, it’s a no-brainer.

Average price: $90
Rating: 93

See Review

The Dalmore 12 Year Sherry Cask Select

This limited release is finished in a mix of Oloroso and PX sherry casks. It’s got the classic Dalmore dessert-y notes of dark chocolate and candied oranges, only taken a step further. It’s nutty, it’s spicy, it’s a bit earthy and salty, there’s even a kiss of smoke. Elegant and rich, it would make for an ideal after-dinner pour.

Average price: $90
Rating: 92

See Review

The Best Scotch Whiskies Over $100

The Glendronach Ode to the Embers

Just as with its Brown-Forman portfolio mate Benriach, Glendronach is more known for its heavily-sherried single malts, but, for some reason in this tasting, it was their peated Scotch that truly hit. Don’t get us wrong, that well-known sherry richness is still prominent, it’s just there’s a tantalizing taste of campfire lingering throughout the entire pour. With bramble notes, dried fruits, and some spicy oak notes, this is one sophisticated sipper.

Average price: $105
Rating: 92

See Review

Glenglassaugh 15 Year Old

This coastal-distilled whisky uses PX sherry casks for its 15 year release. The result is a very red wine-like Scotch with notes of figs, raisins, and blackcurrant. There’s a resinous, pine tree-like quality to the palate and perhaps that’s why the baking spice notes can’t help but make one start thinking about the holidays. Whatever the case, this is a worthy introduction to this still somewhat off-the-radar Highlands distillery.

Average price: $110
Rating: 91

See Review

GlenAllachie 15 Year Old

Finished in a variety of sherry puncheons and hogsheads, this is a total sherry bomb. The nose is all rum-soaked fruit cake and the palate is equally rich and luxurious, with notes of dark cherries, milk chocolate, candied ginger, and rancio.

Average price: $113
Rating: 92

See Review

Single Cask Nation Dailuaine 2010 (Skurnik Selection)

Talk about geeky. This 12-year-old Speyside single malt was selected by one of America’s premier independent bottlers, Single Cask Nation, and then bottled exclusively for its distributor, Skurnik. You’re probably not familiar with the distiller, Dailuaine, which is more commonly utilized in Diageo blends. And that’s a shame because as a single malt, it soars. Aged 8 years in ex-bourbon casks before being finished for 4 more in a PX sherry butt, there’s delicate orchard fruit note on the nose, though the palate is richer, with sticky toffee pudding, dark fruits, and honey-dipped apples. At 57.7 percent ABV, the mouthfeel is rich and almost waxy, with a long, lingering finish.

Average price: $122
Rating: 94

See Review

Nc’nean Organic Huntress Malted Teacake

This experimental, limited release in handsome, recycled glass packaging comes from a small distillery on the Morvern peninsula on the West Coast of Scotland. Made with organic Scottish barley, fermented with Belgian ale yeast, and distilled on 100 percent renewable energy copper pot stills, there’s thankfully enough in the palate that it tastes as good as its ecoconsciousness makes you feel. There’s citrus zest on the nose with a light, fruity palate of lemon cookies and berry jam. It’s maybe a hair too pricy, but good deeds usually are.

Average price: $125
Rating: 92

See Review

Oban Aged 15 Years Port Cask Finish

This limited edition release is the second in the brand’s 15-year cask-finished series (the first, Oban 15 Year Old Cask Strength Sherry Cask Finished, was well-celebrated by us last year). Though not quite as effective as sherry, the port casks likewise elevate Oban’s signature maritime character. Here, the sea salt and earthiness are met, but never outshined, by a juicy, Hi-C fruit punch-like quality. There are wisps of smoke in the background, with some chocolate and baking spice notes. This one is for Oban stans or newcomers to the brand alike.

Average price: $130
Rating: 90

See Review

The ImpEx Collection Ardmore 14 Year

The ImpEx Collection offers top single barrel picks from the founders of ImpEx beverages. This Highland malt presents wonderful maritime notes accented by just a hint of peat smoke. There’s an underlying pastry sweetness — lemon cake, vanilla frosting, honey — that keeps the Scotch in balance, even at a cask strength proof of 59.2 percent ABV. With only 169 total bottles, the price feels like a downright steal in this day and age for what would tie as our highest overall ranked Scotch in this entire tasting.

Average price: $150
Rating: 96

See Review

Glengoyne 18 Year Old

This unpeated Highland single malt is aged in ex-bourbon and first fill ex-Oloroso sherry casks. It’s nutty and a bit spicy with classic sherried notes of stewed fruits and a honey sweetness. It’s certainly good, but compared to other heavy hitters of this age, perhaps less of a value.

Average price: $150
Rating: 91

See Review

The Best Scotch Whiskies Over $200

Highland Park 21 Year Old

This rare release was built from a mere 48 casks of three types: sherry-seasoned American oak quarter casks; refill sherry butts; and first-fill, sherry-seasoned European hogsheads. There is the expected sherry/peat sweet/smoky balance that is beloved in all Highland Park releases, but this offers way more richness, elegance, and complexity, with warming wood notes on the backend and a lingering, baking spice finish.

Average price: $367
Rating: 94

See Review

Tamdhu 21 Year Old Sherry Cask Matured

You possibly haven’t heard of Tamdhu as, until last decade, it was almost entirely used in blends, but this will be the first of two on this year’s list. (We rarely include two whiskies from the same brand unless they are bottled by different companies, as is the case here, and both are truly extraordinary.) This limited release (just 12,000 bottles) from Ian Macleod Distillers is aged exclusively in Oloroso sherry casks, as is now standard for Tamdhu. Another year, another great dram from the Artist series on our list. If last year’s Artist Glenburgie 1995 was our highest overall ranking Scotch, this year sees a Tamdhu distilled in 2006 making it. FAQs

How is Scotch different from whiskey?

Technically speaking, all Scotch is whiskey, though producers in the nation and the industry at large opt to drop the “e” from the word, spelling it “whisky” instead.

What are the different types of Scotch?

In total there are five different Scotch regions: Campbeltown, Highland, Islay, Lowland, and Speyside. While producers in each region share some general similarities in style — almost all Islay whisky is peated, for example — so many factors go into Scotch production that two distillers from the same region may produce vastly different styles of whisky.

What is the proper way to drink Scotch?

Scotch is a very versatile spirit that can be sipped neat, with a few drops of water, on the rocks, or mixed in cocktails.

content:
Like any new hobby, getting into bourbon can be fun and exciting. The category presents a wide swath of delicious expressions for novices to try, and discovering a bottle that particularly grooves with your palate’s sensibilities can often inspire further exploration.

Of course, it costs money to begin your bourbon journey. Fortunately, there are plenty of terrific bourbons on the market that can excite your palate without requiring a full-on splurge. These are the purchases that can turn you from a shiny new hobbyist to a full-throttled enthusiast. To help you discover some of these bottles, we talked to 16 bartenders to find out the best bourbons for beginners to check out. Hopefully, one of these bottles will start your bourbon journey down a smooth and thrilling path.

The best bourbons for beginners, according to bartenders:

  • Four Roses Bourbon
  • Woodford Reserve
  • Old Grand-Dad Bonded Reserve
  • Russell’s Reserve 10
  • Buffalo Trace
  • Maker’s Mark
  • Michter’s US*1 Kentucky Straight Bourbon
  • Basil Hayden
  • Elijah Craig Small Batch
  • Angel’s Envy
  • Eagle Rare 10
  • Bullseye Bourbon
  • Woodford Reserve Double Oaked
  • Old Forester
  • Rebel 100
  • Four Roses Single Barrel

“For someone just getting into bourbon, I would recommend Four Roses because they have a bourbon for nearly every occasion. I like to introduce people to Four Roses because you can start with one bottle and work your way through the lineup. It is a fun way to see how different bourbon can be depending on proof, the recipe, and how you choose to drink it. Their classic bottle, Four Roses Bourbon comes in at 80 proof, which is a great place to start. It also makes a really nice Old Fashioned. Its ‘Small Batch’ bottle is a step up in complexity and is great for neat pours or over the rocks. The ‘Single Barrel’ expressions, though, are my favorite; in my opinion, it’s where you really start to appreciate bourbon as a sipping spirit.” —Hailey Knight, beverage director, Félix Cocktails et Cuisine and La Cave, Charleston, S.C.

“I still stand by Woodford Reserve as the introductory bourbon of choice. It was just coming into fashion as I came of drinking age, and it remains a balance of quality-to-price. Its ability to showcase rickhouse, mashbill, and gentle flavor notes is unparalleled, and it’s as smooth as can be, even by wheated bourbon standards.” —Patrick Marran, general manager, Tracks Raw Bar & Grill, New York City

“If you’re a beginner with some adventure in your heart, I recommend Old Grand-Dad Bonded. I almost always have a bottle nearby because not only is it incredibly reasonably priced, it is my favorite bourbon for an Old Fashioned. The mash bill is high-rye at 27 percent rye, and at 50 percent ABV, she really sings in an Old Fashioned and holds her character longer than others once the ice starts melting. She can also stand up to being over-bittered, or over- or under-sweetened. She basically carries the torch slow and steady for one of the best bourbons out there.” —Nora Furst, co-owner, Buddy, San Francisco

“Choosing a whiskey can be incredibly personal. For a beginner, though, I’d start with a classic bourbon that embodies what bourbon is all about: Russell’s Reserve 10 Year. At 90 proof, it showcases the depth and complexity of well-aged bourbon without overwhelming a new drinker with alcohol heat, making it approachable while still offering plenty to explore.” —Sebastián Moreno, beverage director, Yokai, Greensboro, N.C.

“Buffalo Trace is a great beginner bourbon. It’s super affordable, tastes delicious, and its low rye mash bill promotes drinkability. Perfect for an Old Fashioned or Gold Rush.” —Matty Brodeur, bar lead, Pedalers Fork, Calabasas, Calif.

“Maker’s Mark is an ideal introduction to bourbon because its wheated mash bill creates a softer, sweet profile with less aggressive spice. Notes of caramel, vanilla, cocoa, and gentle baking spice make it approachable neat, on the rocks, or in a cocktail.” —Daniel Navarro, beverage director, CHICA, Las Vegas

“For someone beginning to explore bourbon, I would recommend Michter’s US*1 Kentucky Straight Bourbon. It has enough character to show you what great bourbon can be without being overly aggressive or difficult to understand. You get beautiful notes of caramel, vanilla, and toasted oak, with soft spice and a very smooth finish. Woodford Reserve and Maker’s Mark are also excellent introductions to the category, but for a first bottle, Michter’s has that balance of quality, approachability, and personality that makes you want to keep exploring bourbon.” —Dimitrios Michalopoulos, general manager, Bemelmans Bar, NYC

“When approaching bourbon for the first time you have to decide on what you are looking for. Woodford Reserve is a classic Kentucky Bourbon with the mash consisting of 72 percent corn, a touch of rye, and barley. The sweetness from the corn balances well with the spiced bite of the rye. On the other side of the spectrum is Basil Hayden. It’s a lighter expression of Kentucky bourbon, but it’s also one with a higher amount of rye in the mash bill. For a first-time bourbon drinker to really understand the stylistic differences of bourbon, trying these two choices will allow you to know which direction to go for a bourbon exploration journey!” —Elizabeth Walters, general manager, Hearth and Hill Sugar House, Salt Lake City

“I’d recommend Elijah Craig Small Batch as a great bourbon for beginners. At 94 proof, it’s higher than your typical 80 proof entry-level bourbon, and strong enough to stand up in classic bourbon cocktails. It’s also great on its own neat or with a splash of water for beginners who want to start to appreciate bourbon on its own. It has a corn-heavy mash bill of 78 percent, so it’s on the smooth and sweet side, but not as sweet as a wheated bourbon. It also has some nice spice notes, which are the mark of some of the most sought-after bourbons.” —Bryan Schneider, beverage director, Limusina, NYC

“Angel’s Envy, without hesitation. It’s our house bourbon because it hits that sweet spot between approachable and sophisticated. That port-wine-barrel finish gives you vanilla, caramel, ripe fruit, and spice, with this beautiful roundness that invites you in instead of beating up your palate. For someone discovering bourbon, that matters. I can pour you Angel’s Envy neat, over a big rock, or build you a beautiful Old Fashioned, and the whiskey still shows up. Your first bourbon should make you want a second one — and then make you curious about the whole category. That’s Angel’s Envy.” —German Cruz, beverage director, Red Rooster Harlem, NYC

“For bourbon beginners, I’d start with Eagle Rare 10 Year. It’s approachable, with sweetness coming from a decade in the barrel. You’ll get butterscotch, brown sugar, cherry, leather, and a touch of honey, making it rich without being overwhelming. Eagle Rare can be tough to find these days, but it’s worth trying when you spot it at a whiskey bar or a restaurant.” —Jenny Buchhagen, bartender, Waldorf Astoria Monarch Beach, Dana Point, Calif.

“Bullseye Bourbon is a great entry-level offering. It has all the expected vanilla and oak notes, but it also has a high-rye mash bill which makes it a little peppery. It comes in a liter format, and usually retails for around $40.” —Orlando Franklin McCray, beverage director, Cynthia, NYC

“There are very few bourbons out there that I find more approachable than Woodford Reserve Double Oaked. It’s simply delicious, with a rich vanilla and caramel sweetness and very little of the ethanol heat that can make whiskey intimidating to a beginner. At the same time, there’s enough depth and character to make it just as enjoyable for a seasoned whiskey drinker. It’s accessible, reasonably priced, and versatile enough to earn a permanent spot in just about any liquor cabinet.” —Julian Flores Torres, beverage director, Mode Bar, Santa Ana, Calif.

“A longtime favorite beginner’s bourbon is Old Forester 100 proof. It’s bold enough to stand out in cocktails but also delicious enough on its own to drink neat or with a splash of water to bring down the proof. It isn’t hard to acquire but it also isn’t so ubiquitous that it feels pedestrian. Plus, it’s a good intro to the rest of the fantastic Old Forester catalogue.” —Sam Nellis, head bartender, Silver Lyan, Washington, D.C.

“My top recommendation for anyone wanting to ease into the world of bourbon is Rebel 100 Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey. It covers several bases for beginners. First and foremost, it’s delicious! Its wheated mash bill, similar to that of Maker’s Mark, gives it a softer, smoother character and a velvety mouthfeel that makes it especially approachable for newcomers. At 100 proof, it delivers plenty of flavor, but it comes without an overwhelming alcohol burn. Instead, you’ll find inviting notes of caramel, honey, and biscuit. And perhaps best of all, it’s an affordable introduction to quality bourbon, with a bottle typically priced under $30. For beginners who want something flavorful, smooth, and easy to enjoy without spending a lot, Rebel 100 is an excellent place to start.” —Jeffrey Ambler, bartender, Flight West, Miami

“Four Roses Single Barrel Bourbon is the best introductory bourbon on the market. With a mash bill of 60 percent corn, 35 percent rye, and 5 percent malted barley, this bourbon packs plenty of spicy punch and brings a mellow sweetness to round it out. The lovely brown sugar and vanilla nose is a great invitation to pursue the drink. The palate treats you with flavors of peaches and honey, with a little spicy rye note and some oaky astringency to balance it out. And then the finish — cherry, mint, vanilla — is a very long finish indeed! Sounds too good for a beginner’s bourbon, no? That’s the point. Four Roses Single Barrel hits the affordable price point for someone exploring bourbon, while being complex enough to perk one’s curiosity into coming back for more.” —Mark Bystrom, general manager, Salon Salon, New Orleans

content:
On Tuesday, president Donald Trump announced a plan to ban import of a range of Canadian products, escalating the already tense tariff disputes between the U.S. and its neighbor to the north. The restrictions — which are set to go into effect on Sept. 29 — will encompass alcoholic beverages including wine, spirits, malt beer as well as dairy products and motor parts.

The latest in the ongoing tariff tug-of-war, this proclamation came amid a growing trade conflict between the two countries. In July, Trump threatened to add a 50 percent levy on Canadian products including alcohol, milk, and auto parts, set to go into effect on Aug. 19. After glimpses of a potential negotiation, the U.S. and Canada failed to reach an agreement, and the tariffs took effect on Aug. 22. In response, Canada announced retaliatory levies on $20 billion of U.S. goods, which began on Tuesday and spurred Trump’s announcement of the forthcoming ban.

The Trump administration’s strong-arming began in April 2024 with the announcement of the Liberation Day tariffs, to which Canada responded with a province-wide ban, stripping U.S. alcohol products from retail and bar shelves across the country. Canada’s booze ban contributed to considerable dings to the export revenue from the U.S. wine, beer, and spirits industries in 2025.

Whether there is room for trade negotiations remains to be seen. Officials from both countries — reliable trading partners — remained steadfast in their hopes for a potential deal, though no efforts have been made to advance negotiations yet.

content:
Campania, the southern Italian region on the Tyrrhenian Sea, is perhaps best known for Aglianico, the marvelous red variety that is sometimes referred to as “the Barolo of the South.” If you haven’t tried Aglianico, here are some recommendations from my column earlier this year.

Beyond Aglianico, Campania, with its volcanic soils deposited by Mount Vesuvius, offers several notable but lesser-known white varieties that produce some of the more exciting wines on the southern Italian landscape.

With many wine lovers gravitating toward lighter, lower-alcohol whites, Campania’s offerings are an obvious choice and deserve more consideration. They are mostly unoaked and aged in stainless steel tanks.

Along with Campania’s soils, its hilly terrain provides a cooling influence that preserves acidity in the grapes. This translates to fresh and flavorful wines that pair well with fish, shellfish, cheeses, all manner of vegetables, and other lighter foods.

Among them is Fiano, the grape of the celebrated Fiano di Avellino denomination, named after the city and province of Avellino. With its crisp acidity, Fiano is marked by its freshness but also its vivid fruit, floral, and herbal notes. While relatively light, it can be complex and multi-layered.

Other notable white varieties from Campania include Greco and Falanghina. As the name suggests, Greco is thought to have originated in Greece, and in the top Greco di Tufo denomination, Tufo refers to tuffa, the chalky, compressed volcanic soil that gives the wine its minerality. Falanghina, which may have also come from Greece, may be slightly less complex but produces refreshing wines for everyday drinking. There’s also an example of the ancient Coda di Volpe variety on the list below.

Many of Campania’s most prominent wine regions are near Mount Vesuvius, an active volcano, and Mount Taburno. Beyond Avellino and the noted Irpinia region, other important areas include the province of Benevento and its Sannio subregion.

The white wines of Campania sometimes remind me of Etna Biancos, the high-acid, mineral-driven wines from the Mount Etna region of Sicily. Although the grapes are different, the style is similar: refreshing, textured volcanic wines that represent some of the better white-wine values.

Here are nine of the best white wines from Campania.

Tenuta Scuotto Fiano di Avellino 2023

There’s a nice richness to this Fiano, with aromas and flavors of peach, honey, and herbs, most notably a touch of mint. There’s also an almond hint and a mineral backdrop. Starting with the 2026 vintage, the property is certified organic. While many people think these wines should be drunk within a year or two of bottling, this one suggests that they can develop a richer character as they age.

Price: $20
Buy This Wine

Villa Matilde Greco di Tufo di Altavilla 2024

This crisp, lemony wine has good complexity with a green apple note joining the citrus. An herbal touch offsets the fruit and the wine is marked by a long, mineral finish. Easy to drink, refreshing, and memorable.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Cantine Iorio Falanghina Beneventano 2025

Cantine Iorio only produces Aglianico and Falanghina, and this Falanghina from the province of Benevento is grown in limestone and clay soil. Light straw in color, its rich fruit evokes honeydew melon with touches of honeysuckle, white flowers, almond, white pepper, and menthol. Aged for four months in stainless steel tanks, it’s a “summer” wine you’ll enjoy all year.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Cautiero ‘Trois’ Greco 2023

Cautiero, a winery located near Mount Taberno, farms organically and uses four or five days of skin contact for its white wines. This golden-colored orange wine is bursting with concentrated fruit flavors, including candied apple, peach, apricot, lemon, and hints of grapefruit and honey. The flavors are supported by a mild tannic grip and excellent acidity.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Contrada Fiano di Avellino 2024

This fresh, delicately savory wine has a nice richness that frames aromas and flavors of lemon-lime and a touch of honey. Hints of tomato leaf, herbs, and saline provide interesting accents along with the long, mineral finish. The ’23 is being sold here.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Fattoria La Rivolta Fiano Taburno Sannio

Luscious fruit is punctuated by pronounced minerality in this notable Fiano. There’s a nice round quality to the wine, which shows apple, strawberry, and orange notes with hints of thyme and white flowers. La Rivolta has used organic farming practices for almost three decades.

Price: $25
Buy This Wine

Fattoria La Rivolta Coda di Volpe Taburno Sannio 2024

Fattoria La Rivolta also makes a notable expression of Coda di Volpe — a lesser-known white variety in Campania — showcasing its fresh and elegant profile. Flint and almond hints punctuate aromas and flavors of white peach, apricot, and a touch of vanilla. The wine has a nice roundness and a long, mineral finish.

Price: $21
Buy This Wine

Iovine Falanghina 2024

This is an excellent, under-$20 Falanghina marked by its freshness, ripe fruit, and a slight spritz when first poured. Aromas and flavors of citrus, mainly orange, are joined by pineapple and herbal notes that lead to a long, mineral finish.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Villa Matilde Fiano di Avellino ‘Montelapio’ 2024

This is an enjoyable, easy-drinking wine that could easily be your house white for casual sipping or pairing with simple fish and chicken dishes. It offers green and red apple notes, a hint of citrus, and the region’s signature minerality. Crisp and refreshing.

Price: $23

content:
On Thursday, alcohol distributor Southern Glazer’s announced that it reached a resolution with the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Alcohol and Tobacco Trade Bureau (TTB) in a longstanding investigation related to improper payments and bribery. In the deal, Southern agreed to pay $12.5 million. With this resolution the DOJ has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with the distributor, and the TTB agreed to take no further action regarding this case.

Last year, the U.S. government opened a federal investigation into the distributor regarding misconduct that occurred from 2016 to 2024. Former employees allegedly handed out cash payments, gift cards, luxury goods, golf trips, flights, and resort bookings for retailers in California for better shelf placement of Southern Glazer’s products and other benefits in return. The DOJ also says the company took out false invoices to conceal the payments.

“We are gratified to resolve the investigation in this fashion, and to be able to focus on earning the trust of our customers, supplier partners, and employees through ethical business practices, strong compliance oversight, and accountability at every level of the organization,” Southern Glazer’s president and chief executive officer Wayne Chaplin said in a statement released on Thursday evening.

In addition to the $12.5 million payment, Southern Glazer’s agreed to reinforce the company’s internal guardrails to prevent future misconduct. In the release, the company stated it had already made inroads to improve its TTB compliance after the federal investigation surfaced and prior to reaching the agreement. Southern Glazer’s claims it bolstered its staff and implemented proactive auditing, among other measures. The statement also suggests the non-prosecution agreement includes “other obligations over the next two years,” though the company did not disclose what those entail.

“This case serves as an important reminder that industry members are accountable not only for their own conduct, but also for the actions taken on their behalf by third party affiliates,” Anthony P. Gledhill, assistant administrator of field operations for the TTB said in a statement from the DOJ. “Third parties, likewise, are responsible for any illegal activities they carry out on behalf of an industry member.”

This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. News to know:

  • France braces for a record low harvest: After a growing season tempered by droughts and wildfires, producers in the country are expecting this year’s harvest to produce the lowest yields in 30 years. The French agriculture ministry forecasts a total of roughly 900 million gallons to be produced from this year’s harvest, a 6 percent dip year-over-year and a 17 percent drop from the average volume measured across 2021 to 2025.
  • Sapporo stokes the U.S.-Canada tariff fire: The Japanese brewer announced its plans to shift some of its brewing operations to the U.S. from Canada following the onset of a 50 percent tariff on Canadian beer. The move also comes after Trump issued a ban on Canadian alcohol imports, which is set to begin Sept. 29.
  • Dentist slashes world record Champagne sabrage: Swiss dentist Mirko Bozin broke the record for the number of Champagne bottles sabred in one minute. Bozin blew the tops off of 118 bottles in 60 seconds at a cutthroat tournament in Neuchâtel, Switzerland, breaking the previous record of 96 bottles that had been set just three months prior.
  • Kendall Jenner’s second bev-alc foray: The supermodel acquired a minority stake in U.K.-based functional beverage brand Trip.Trip launched in 2019 with cannabis-derived products but has since shifted its focus to other adaptogens, including non-psychedelic mushrooms.

Product releases to watch:

  • A new seat at the aperitivo table: The Campari Group, which dominates the Spritz sector with brands like Aperol under its wing, introduced a new aperitivo to the U.S.: Sarti. Though it was first founded in 1885, this marks its first appearance stateside, landing in markets nationwide. The blush-colored liquor blends blood orange, passion fruit, and mango flavors into a sweeter profile than the bitter qualities of Campari and Aperol.

content:
In 2026, it’s hard to think of a food that hasn’t been Dirty Martini-ified. The rise of the savory drinks trend over the past few years brought variations spiked with pickle brine, sungold tomatoes, and MSG, and flavors inspired by sour cream and onion chips, Greek salad, and brioche.

At Titán, the new bar and restaurant in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood, the tart, acidic flavors of escabeche are given the Martini treatment in the Dirty Root. But in making the drink, co-owner Ivy Mix and head bartender Sergio Sarmiento weren’t trying to follow the all-things food fad. Instead, they were looking to capture the signature briny flavors of a classic Dirty Martini while paying homage to the flavors of northern Mexico.

Titán is a collaboration between Mix and co-owner chef Alan Delgado. Both established themselves as masterminds of Brooklyn’s food and beverage scene in their own rights — Mix at bars like the beloved (and now-closed) Leyenda and Whoopsie Daisy and Delgado at Fort Greene’s Los Burritos Juárez, known for its hand-rolled flour tortillas and long lines.

Mix likes to think of a cocktail menu like a vinyl album: The whole should be better than the sum of its parts. Where the songs together to form a cohesive story in an old-school LP, the various drinks on a single cocktail menu should sing in harmony.

“When I make a menu, I have a spreadsheet of what kind of flavors we’re using, what kind of spirits we’re using, so I can see that I’m kind of covering the entire drink spectrum,” she says.

The Dirty Root was Titán’s answer to the Dirty Martini. While diners can order the classics, Mix likes to have her own versions of popular cocktails at the ready to point guests toward something new and unique.

“There are certain boxes that I want to check, so when people come in and ask for, for example, an Espresso Martini, we can say, ‘Do you want to try ours?’” she says. “The Dirty Root was the Dirty Martini box that we wanted to check.”

Though the Dirty Root resembles a Dirty Martini in its look and briny flavor, the ingredients are a far cry from the drink’s vodka-and-olive-brine roots. Bacanora — an agave-based liquor from northern Mexico’s Sonora region — and blanco tequila act as the base of the cocktail, with dry vermouth, carrot eau de vie, and carrot liqueur playing supporting roles. Rather than relying on the classic olives for the savory punch, Mix and Sarmiento looked to escabache, a piquant and spicy ensemble of pickled vegetables, usually including peppers, carrots, and onions, that’s a staple in many Mexican households.

“In pretty much all of the houses in Mexico, they have homemade chiles and vegetables in vinegar,” he says. “If you only have tortillas and beans, you can make tacos by adding the escabeche.”

Once the two brainstormed their vision for a Dirty Martini riff, Sarmiento began experimenting with making a carrot vinegar at home. While the root vegetables’ juice brings a burst of flavor on their own, Sarmiento needed to find a mixture that would complement the cocktail’s combination of liquors. After a series of trial-and-error, he landed on a blend of carrot juice, vinegar, sugar, and salt, with touches of turmeric and ginger.

“Then we put it all together, and you have this earthy, savory, northern Mexico-style Martini,” Mix says.

The striking drink presents in the glass with a bright orange hue and is served with a sidecar boasting a trio of garnishes: a lemon twist, a pickled carrot spear, and a cocktail onion. Mix shares that its appealing presentation spurs an onslaught of orders when it makes its way across the room, suggesting that it has somewhat of a “fajita effect” with customers.

“People definitely do that to this drink because the glass is sexy, it comes with a little sidecar, and the color is just really kind of light and beautiful,” she says.

The Dirty Root’s eye-catching appearance and complex flavor profile has propelled it to become one of Titán’s most popular orders. And consumers’ recent infatuation with Martinis — especially food-inspired ones — doesn’t hurt. But in conceptualizing the cocktail, Mix and Sarmiento never sought out to meet some kind of trend.

“There’s this fad going on right now, which is fine, where everything tastes like food,” Mix says. “Taking a food element was not the point. The inspiration for this drink is all of the flavors of the north of Mexico.”

content:
Is it possible that 2026 could eventually be looked back on as the make-or-break year for Scotch whisky?

In July, the U.S. finally lifted its 15 month tariff on Scotch, one that had contributed to a 15 percent decline in exports to this country, one of Scotland’s biggest international markets. Meanwhile, a new ​​U.K.–India free trade agreement introduced that same month could likewise prove transformational in opening up the world’s largest whisky market to more affordable Scotch.

And yet, many distilleries still remain on a sort of “pause” — Diageo and Brown-Forman operations of note — after the market became oversaturated post-pandemic, with a historic glut of liquid still building. Others, like Clynelish, have closed their visitors’ centers due to a lack of tourist interest.

On the positive, though, it seems that, thanks to a so-called “premiumization fatigue,” distilleries are focusing less on overpriced and ostentatious “clickbait” releases — your $200K Macallans for instance — and more on good, affordable, drinking Scotch. Indeed, this year’s tasting saw plenty of sub-$100, over-a-decade age-stated releases that snobs and newbs alike would be more than happy to have in their home bars.

From entry level offerings from the biggest names to more elevated releases from sleeper brands, exciting independent bottlings and a whole bunch of sherry bombs, here are VinePair’s 25 best Scotch whiskies for 2026.

Why You Should Trust VinePair

Every year, VinePair conducts dozens of tastings for our “Buy This Booze” product roundups, highlighting the best bottles across the world’s most popular wine and spirits categories.
Within this scope, VinePair’s tasting and editorial staff samples thousands of bottles every year.

This ensures we have a close eye on what’s new and exciting. Crucially, it also provides us with the context needed to distinguish the simply good from the truly great, whether from a quality or value-for-money perspective — or both.

Ultimately, our mission is to offer a clear, reliable source of information for drinkers, providing an overview applicable to day-to-day buying and drinking. Learn more about VinePair’s tastings and reviews department here.

How We Taste

We believe in tasting all products as our readers typically would: with full knowledge of the producer and — importantly — price. Our tastings are therefore not conducted blind.

For this Scotch roundup, all expressions were sampled in Glencairn glasses and allowed to rest for five minutes prior to tasting. We then evaluated the aromas, flavors, texture, and finish of each whisky. Unless there was something notably off or worrying about a whisky’s appearance — and on this occasion we encountered no such examples — we did not evaluate the products from a visual perspective.

How We Compiled This List

In order to provide our readers with the most comprehensive and thoroughly tested list of the best Scotch whiskies to buy, VinePair invited producers, distributors, and PR firms working on their behalf to send samples for consideration. These bottles were submitted free of charge — producers didn’t pay to submit nor did VinePair pay for the products. All were requested with the clear understanding that submission does not guarantee inclusion in the final list.

Not only would such an agreement contradict our editorial ethics and samples policy, it simply wouldn’t be possible to include everything we received. For this roundup, we tasted over 70 new submissions and also retasted more than a dozen bottles that were sent to VinePair throughout the course of the prior 12 months and that we were able to confirm are still available in retail channels.

During tasting, we assigned a score to each product on a 100-point scale based on the quality and intensity of its aromas, flavors, texture, and finish. Then we reviewed all scores and compiled an editorially driven list that meets our criteria of 25 best Scotch whiskies to buy right now. It’s important to note that these are not just the highest-scoring bottles we tasted this year. Instead, this list showcases the best examples of Scotch across every price and for every scenario — because while price is completely objective, “affordability” is not.

The 25 Best Scotch Whiskies to Drink in 2026

The Best Scotch for Beginners

Glenmorangie Original 12

If “GlenMo” is no longer all that exciting to Scotch nerds, even they would have to agree there’s really nothing to dislike about this entry-level dram, especially at such a friendly price. It’s citrusy on the nose, with vanilla and sweet stone fruit on the palate, leading to a mildly spicy (cinnamon candy) finish. Despite the lower proof (40 percent ABV), there’s a creaminess of mouthfeel that makes this endlessly drinkable whether neat, on a cube, or even in cocktails. What can we say? This is just flawless single malt and a great place for a Scotch beginner to get started.

The Best Blended Scotch

Compass Box Orchard House

Year after year, this category continues to be owned by Compass Box. (Quite frankly, we get very few blended Scotch submissions these days.) But despite the lack of competition, Orchard House shone brightly this year. This blend of single malt whiskies from Caol Ila, Clynelish, and several undisclosed distilleries was designed to be fruit forward as the name suggests and, indeed, it is apple-y on the palate, to the point of being almost brandy-like. A tad one-note, but never not delicate and delicious, this is a shining example of mastering a flavor profile through skillful blending.

Kilchoman Sanaig

One of the more slept-on distilleries on the island of Islay, Kilchoman quietly continues to put out some of the best releases in the region. Named after an inlet on the island, Sanaig is produced from a vatting of ex-bourbon and sherry casks, specifically Oloroso. The dried fruit/baking spice barrel notes meld beautifully with the smoke, making for a peated whiskey that is both accessible to newbies to the category, yet pleasing in complexity to longtime fans.

Much milder in peated notes than its Islay brethren, the nose is floral and almost saison-like, though the palate is rich in toffee, maple syrup, and pipe tobacco. FAQs

How is Scotch different from whiskey?

Technically speaking, all Scotch is whiskey, though producers in the nation and the industry at large opt to drop the “e” from the word, spelling it “whisky” instead.

What are the different types of Scotch?

In total there are five different Scotch regions: Campbeltown, Highland, Islay, Lowland, and Speyside. While producers in each region share some general similarities in style — almost all Islay whisky is peated, for example — so many factors go into Scotch production that two distillers from the same region may produce vastly different styles of whisky.

What is the proper way to drink Scotch?

Scotch is a very versatile spirit that can be sipped neat, with a few drops of water, on the rocks, or mixed in cocktails.

content:
Like any new hobby, getting into bourbon can be fun and exciting. The category presents a wide swath of delicious expressions for novices to try, and discovering a bottle that particularly grooves with your palate’s sensibilities can often inspire further exploration.

Of course, it costs money to begin your bourbon journey. Fortunately, there are plenty of terrific bourbons on the market that can excite your palate without requiring a full-on splurge. These are the purchases that can turn you from a shiny new hobbyist to a full-throttled enthusiast. To help you discover some of these bottles, we talked to 16 bartenders to find out the best bourbons for beginners to check out. Hopefully, one of these bottles will start your bourbon journey down a smooth and thrilling path.

The best bourbons for beginners, according to bartenders:

  • Four Roses Bourbon
  • Woodford Reserve
  • Old Grand-Dad Bonded Reserve
  • Russell’s Reserve 10
  • Buffalo Trace
  • Maker’s Mark
  • Michter’s US*1 Kentucky Straight Bourbon
  • Basil Hayden
  • Elijah Craig Small Batch
  • Angel’s Envy
  • Eagle Rare 10
  • Bullseye Bourbon
  • Woodford Reserve Double Oaked
  • Old Forester
  • Rebel 100
  • Four Roses Single Barrel

“For someone just getting into bourbon, I would recommend Four Roses because they have a bourbon for nearly every occasion. I like to introduce people to Four Roses because you can start with one bottle and work your way through the lineup. It is a fun way to see how different bourbon can be depending on proof, the recipe, and how you choose to drink it. Their classic bottle, Four Roses Bourbon comes in at 80 proof, which is a great place to start. It also makes a really nice Old Fashioned. Its ‘Small Batch’ bottle is a step up in complexity and is great for neat pours or over the rocks. The ‘Single Barrel’ expressions, though, are my favorite; in my opinion, it’s where you really start to appreciate bourbon as a sipping spirit.” —Hailey Knight, beverage director, Félix Cocktails et Cuisine and La Cave, Charleston, S.C.

“I still stand by Woodford Reserve as the introductory bourbon of choice. It was just coming into fashion as I came of drinking age, and it remains a balance of quality-to-price. Its ability to showcase rickhouse, mashbill, and gentle flavor notes is unparalleled, and it’s as smooth as can be, even by wheated bourbon standards.” —Patrick Marran, general manager, Tracks Raw Bar & Grill, New York City

“If you’re a beginner with some adventure in your heart, I recommend Old Grand-Dad Bonded. I almost always have a bottle nearby because not only is it incredibly reasonably priced, it is my favorite bourbon for an Old Fashioned. The mash bill is high-rye at 27 percent rye, and at 50 percent ABV, she really sings in an Old Fashioned and holds her character longer than others once the ice starts melting. She can also stand up to being over-bittered, or over- or under-sweetened. She basically carries the torch slow and steady for one of the best bourbons out there.” —Nora Furst, co-owner, Buddy, San Francisco

“Choosing a whiskey can be incredibly personal. For a beginner, though, I’d start with a classic bourbon that embodies what bourbon is all about: Russell’s Reserve 10 Year. At 90 proof, it showcases the depth and complexity of well-aged bourbon without overwhelming a new drinker with alcohol heat, making it approachable while still offering plenty to explore.” —Sebastián Moreno, beverage director, Yokai, Greensboro, N.C.

“Buffalo Trace is a great beginner bourbon. It’s super affordable, tastes delicious, and its low rye mash bill promotes drinkability. Perfect for an Old Fashioned or Gold Rush.” —Matty Brodeur, bar lead, Pedalers Fork, Calabasas, Calif.

“Maker’s Mark is an ideal introduction to bourbon because its wheated mash bill creates a softer, sweet profile with less aggressive spice. Notes of caramel, vanilla, cocoa, and gentle baking spice make it approachable neat, on the rocks, or in a cocktail.” —Daniel Navarro, beverage director, CHICA, Las Vegas

“For someone beginning to explore bourbon, I would recommend Michter’s US*1 Kentucky Straight Bourbon. It has enough character to show you what great bourbon can be without being overly aggressive or difficult to understand. You get beautiful notes of caramel, vanilla, and toasted oak, with soft spice and a very smooth finish. Woodford Reserve and Maker’s Mark are also excellent introductions to the category, but for a first bottle, Michter’s has that balance of quality, approachability, and personality that makes you want to keep exploring bourbon.” —Dimitrios Michalopoulos, general manager, Bemelmans Bar, NYC

“When approaching bourbon for the first time you have to decide on what you are looking for. Woodford Reserve is a classic Kentucky Bourbon with the mash consisting of 72 percent corn, a touch of rye, and barley. The sweetness from the corn balances well with the spiced bite of the rye. On the other side of the spectrum is Basil Hayden. It’s a lighter expression of Kentucky bourbon, but it’s also one with a higher amount of rye in the mash bill. For a first-time bourbon drinker to really understand the stylistic differences of bourbon, trying these two choices will allow you to know which direction to go for a bourbon exploration journey!” —Elizabeth Walters, general manager, Hearth and Hill Sugar House, Salt Lake City

“I’d recommend Elijah Craig Small Batch as a great bourbon for beginners. At 94 proof, it’s higher than your typical 80 proof entry-level bourbon, and strong enough to stand up in classic bourbon cocktails. It’s also great on its own neat or with a splash of water for beginners who want to start to appreciate bourbon on its own. It has a corn-heavy mash bill of 78 percent, so it’s on the smooth and sweet side, but not as sweet as a wheated bourbon. It also has some nice spice notes, which are the mark of some of the most sought-after bourbons.” —Bryan Schneider, beverage director, Limusina, NYC

“Angel’s Envy, without hesitation. It’s our house bourbon because it hits that sweet spot between approachable and sophisticated. That port-wine-barrel finish gives you vanilla, caramel, ripe fruit, and spice, with this beautiful roundness that invites you in instead of beating up your palate. For someone discovering bourbon, that matters. I can pour you Angel’s Envy neat, over a big rock, or build you a beautiful Old Fashioned, and the whiskey still shows up. Your first bourbon should make you want a second one — and then make you curious about the whole category. That’s Angel’s Envy.” —German Cruz, beverage director, Red Rooster Harlem, NYC

“For bourbon beginners, I’d start with Eagle Rare 10 Year. It’s approachable, with sweetness coming from a decade in the barrel. You’ll get butterscotch, brown sugar, cherry, leather, and a touch of honey, making it rich without being overwhelming. Eagle Rare can be tough to find these days, but it’s worth trying when you spot it at a whiskey bar or a restaurant.” —Jenny Buchhagen, bartender, Waldorf Astoria Monarch Beach, Dana Point, Calif.

“Bullseye Bourbon is a great entry-level offering. It has all the expected vanilla and oak notes, but it also has a high-rye mash bill which makes it a little peppery. It comes in a liter format, and usually retails for around $40.” —Orlando Franklin McCray, beverage director, Cynthia, NYC

“There are very few bourbons out there that I find more approachable than Woodford Reserve Double Oaked. It’s simply delicious, with a rich vanilla and caramel sweetness and very little of the ethanol heat that can make whiskey intimidating to a beginner. At the same time, there’s enough depth and character to make it just as enjoyable for a seasoned whiskey drinker. It’s accessible, reasonably priced, and versatile enough to earn a permanent spot in just about any liquor cabinet.” —Julian Flores Torres, beverage director, Mode Bar, Santa Ana, Calif.

“A longtime favorite beginner’s bourbon is Old Forester 100 proof. It’s bold enough to stand out in cocktails but also delicious enough on its own to drink neat or with a splash of water to bring down the proof. It isn’t hard to acquire but it also isn’t so ubiquitous that it feels pedestrian. Plus, it’s a good intro to the rest of the fantastic Old Forester catalogue.” —Sam Nellis, head bartender, Silver Lyan, Washington, D.C.

“My top recommendation for anyone wanting to ease into the world of bourbon is Rebel 100 Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey. It covers several bases for beginners. First and foremost, it’s delicious! Its wheated mash bill, similar to that of Maker’s Mark, gives it a softer, smoother character and a velvety mouthfeel that makes it especially approachable for newcomers. At 100 proof, it delivers plenty of flavor, but it comes without an overwhelming alcohol burn. Instead, you’ll find inviting notes of caramel, honey, and biscuit. And perhaps best of all, it’s an affordable introduction to quality bourbon, with a bottle typically priced under $30. For beginners who want something flavorful, smooth, and easy to enjoy without spending a lot, Rebel 100 is an excellent place to start.” —Jeffrey Ambler, bartender, Flight West, Miami

“Four Roses Single Barrel Bourbon is the best introductory bourbon on the market. With a mash bill of 60 percent corn, 35 percent rye, and 5 percent malted barley, this bourbon packs plenty of spicy punch and brings a mellow sweetness to round it out. The lovely brown sugar and vanilla nose is a great invitation to pursue the drink. The palate treats you with flavors of peaches and honey, with a little spicy rye note and some oaky astringency to balance it out. And then the finish — cherry, mint, vanilla — is a very long finish indeed! Sounds too good for a beginner’s bourbon, no? That’s the point. Four Roses Single Barrel hits the affordable price point for someone exploring bourbon, while being complex enough to perk one’s curiosity into coming back for more.” —Mark Bystrom, general manager, Salon Salon, New Orleans

content:
On Tuesday, president Donald Trump announced a plan to ban import of a range of Canadian products, escalating the already tense tariff disputes between the U.S. and its neighbor to the north. The restrictions — which are set to go into effect on Sept. 29 — will encompass alcoholic beverages including wine, spirits, malt beer as well as dairy products and motor parts.

The latest in the ongoing tariff tug-of-war, this proclamation came amid a growing trade conflict between the two countries. In July, Trump threatened to add a 50 percent levy on Canadian products including alcohol, milk, and auto parts, set to go into effect on Aug. 19. After glimpses of a potential negotiation, the U.S. and Canada failed to reach an agreement, and the tariffs took effect on Aug. 22. In response, Canada announced retaliatory levies on $20 billion of U.S. goods, which began on Tuesday and spurred Trump’s announcement of the forthcoming ban.

The Trump administration’s strong-arming began in April 2024 with the announcement of the Liberation Day tariffs, to which Canada responded with a province-wide ban, stripping U.S. alcohol products from retail and bar shelves across the country. Canada’s booze ban contributed to considerable dings to the export revenue from the U.S. wine, beer, and spirits industries in 2025.

Whether there is room for trade negotiations remains to be seen. Officials from both countries — reliable trading partners — remained steadfast in their hopes for a potential deal, though no efforts have been made to advance negotiations yet.

content:
Campania, the southern Italian region on the Tyrrhenian Sea, is perhaps best known for Aglianico, the marvelous red variety that is sometimes referred to as “the Barolo of the South.” If you haven’t tried Aglianico, here are some recommendations from my column earlier this year.

Beyond Aglianico, Campania, with its volcanic soils deposited by Mount Vesuvius, offers several notable but lesser-known white varieties that produce some of the more exciting wines on the southern Italian landscape.

With many wine lovers gravitating toward lighter, lower-alcohol whites, Campania’s offerings are an obvious choice and deserve more consideration. They are mostly unoaked and aged in stainless steel tanks.

Along with Campania’s soils, its hilly terrain provides a cooling influence that preserves acidity in the grapes. This translates to fresh and flavorful wines that pair well with fish, shellfish, cheeses, all manner of vegetables, and other lighter foods.

Among them is Fiano, the grape of the celebrated Fiano di Avellino denomination, named after the city and province of Avellino. With its crisp acidity, Fiano is marked by its freshness but also its vivid fruit, floral, and herbal notes. While relatively light, it can be complex and multi-layered.

Other notable white varieties from Campania include Greco and Falanghina. As the name suggests, Greco is thought to have originated in Greece, and in the top Greco di Tufo denomination, Tufo refers to tuffa, the chalky, compressed volcanic soil that gives the wine its minerality. Falanghina, which may have also come from Greece, may be slightly less complex but produces refreshing wines for everyday drinking. There’s also an example of the ancient Coda di Volpe variety on the list below.

Many of Campania’s most prominent wine regions are near Mount Vesuvius, an active volcano, and Mount Taburno. Beyond Avellino and the noted Irpinia region, other important areas include the province of Benevento and its Sannio subregion.

The white wines of Campania sometimes remind me of Etna Biancos, the high-acid, mineral-driven wines from the Mount Etna region of Sicily. Although the grapes are different, the style is similar: refreshing, textured volcanic wines that represent some of the better white-wine values.

Here are nine of the best white wines from Campania.

Tenuta Scuotto Fiano di Avellino 2023

There’s a nice richness to this Fiano, with aromas and flavors of peach, honey, and herbs, most notably a touch of mint. There’s also an almond hint and a mineral backdrop. Starting with the 2026 vintage, the property is certified organic. While many people think these wines should be drunk within a year or two of bottling, this one suggests that they can develop a richer character as they age.

Price: $20
Buy This Wine

Villa Matilde Greco di Tufo di Altavilla 2024

This crisp, lemony wine has good complexity with a green apple note joining the citrus. An herbal touch offsets the fruit and the wine is marked by a long, mineral finish. Easy to drink, refreshing, and memorable.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Cantine Iorio Falanghina Beneventano 2025

Cantine Iorio only produces Aglianico and Falanghina, and this Falanghina from the province of Benevento is grown in limestone and clay soil. Light straw in color, its rich fruit evokes honeydew melon with touches of honeysuckle, white flowers, almond, white pepper, and menthol. Aged for four months in stainless steel tanks, it’s a “summer” wine you’ll enjoy all year.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Cautiero ‘Trois’ Greco 2023

Cautiero, a winery located near Mount Taberno, farms organically and uses four or five days of skin contact for its white wines. This golden-colored orange wine is bursting with concentrated fruit flavors, including candied apple, peach, apricot, lemon, and hints of grapefruit and honey. The flavors are supported by a mild tannic grip and excellent acidity.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Contrada Fiano di Avellino 2024

This fresh, delicately savory wine has a nice richness that frames aromas and flavors of lemon-lime and a touch of honey. Hints of tomato leaf, herbs, and saline provide interesting accents along with the long, mineral finish. The ’23 is being sold here.

Price: $23
Buy This Wine

Fattoria La Rivolta Fiano Taburno Sannio

Luscious fruit is punctuated by pronounced minerality in this notable Fiano. There’s a nice round quality to the wine, which shows apple, strawberry, and orange notes with hints of thyme and white flowers. La Rivolta has used organic farming practices for almost three decades.

Price: $25
Buy This Wine

Fattoria La Rivolta Coda di Volpe Taburno Sannio 2024

Fattoria La Rivolta also makes a notable expression of Coda di Volpe — a lesser-known white variety in Campania — showcasing its fresh and elegant profile. Flint and almond hints punctuate aromas and flavors of white peach, apricot, and a touch of vanilla. The wine has a nice roundness and a long, mineral finish.

Price: $21
Buy This Wine

Iovine Falanghina 2024

This is an excellent, under-$20 Falanghina marked by its freshness, ripe fruit, and a slight spritz when first poured. Aromas and flavors of citrus, mainly orange, are joined by pineapple and herbal notes that lead to a long, mineral finish.

Price: $18
Buy This Wine

Villa Matilde Fiano di Avellino ‘Montelapio’ 2024

This is an enjoyable, easy-drinking wine that could easily be your house white for casual sipping or pairing with simple fish and chicken dishes. It offers green and red apple notes, a hint of citrus, and the region’s signature minerality. Crisp and refreshing.

Price: $23
